newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Canada bank shows confidence in Argentina-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Canada bank shows confidence in Argentina-analysts.

text.p: Canada's Bank of Nova Scotia became the latest foreign company to demonstrate a growing confidence in the Argentine banking sector with news on Monday that it will raise its stake in Banco Quilmes to at least 95 percent.

Bank of Nova Scotia, which has owned 25 percent of Quilmes for two years, decided to buy the Fiorito-Bianchi family's controlling 70 percent for an undisclosed amount, the Argentine bank said. Small shareholders are expected to sell it their remaining five percent.

"The fact that Nova Scotia is buying all of Quilmes is a reinforcement of the foreign presence and solidity of the financial system," said economist Carlos Perez of the private analysts' group Fundacion Capital.
The past two months have brought sweeping changes to the Argentine banking sector, with just one of the country's top 10 insitutions remaining in Argentina hands.

HSBC Holdings Plc bought Roberts Group, which includes Banco Roberts. Spain's Banco Bilbao Viscaya acquired 72 percent of Banco de Credito Argentino through its Argentine-controlled Banco Frances, and Spain's Banco Santander has taken control of Banco Rio.

"With what is going on in the market, it was a question of, "Do we want to be a big bank or a small bank?" Quilmes has the potential to be a big bank," one member of the Quilmes/Scotia directorate told Reuters.

Banco Quilmes is a smaller player, ranking 13th in the country in terms of deposits and 15th measured by loans. Still, it has 86 branches, giving it good retail banking prospectives. It also owns 17 percent of private pension fund Maxima.

Full details of the deal, including how much it is worth, are not to be announced until Wednesday, but one director told Reuters: "Clearly we are going to continue being a retail, commercial and corporate bank."

He said the new Canadian owners, who operate in 48 countries with over 34,000 employees worldwide, plan to keep up the "growth stategy in place since the next generation of the Fiorito-Bianchi family came in six years ago."

There had been speculation for weeks that Bank of Nova Scotia would raise its stake in Banco Quilmes to around 51 percent. Analysts said the size and timing of the deal clearly boosted confidence in the Argentine banking sector.

"Nova Scotia are a special case because they were already here. At first they came timidly, but now they're no longer interested in having Argentine partners, which means they feel comfortable here and they want it all," said Sergio Galvan, head of research at Bansud.
Galvan said the Canadians' strategy was likely to concentrate on the retail banking business, "which is where there is most margin left and most room to impose prices."
But analysts said it was still not clear how long it would take for the heightened competition to benefit the consumer with in lower lending rates and banking charges.
"There is also still the question of when Argentine bank depositors will start looking at which bank offers them half a percentage point more interest," said Galvan.

Analysts said the market's attention is now likely to be entirely focused on the prospects for the only top Argentine bank still locally-owned -- Banco Galicia, which has so far resisted the foreign buying frenzy.
